sections.heading: Praising your love shown in Jesus
sections.text: Gracious God, my heart praises you for the astonishing love you have shown me in Jesus. He is your beloved Son, and yet for me he became human, was rejected, carried sin, and died on the cross. In him, your grace toward rebels like me has gone beyond anything I could have imagined. Father, teach me to love you in response to that kind of love.
theological_themes: God’s love is most clearly revealed in the giving of his Son for sinners.
Jesus is both the beloved Son of the Father and the crucified sin-bearer for the guilty.
The right response to redeeming love is worship and love back to God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul grounds God’s love not in human worthiness but in Christ’s death for the ungodly. This supports the prayer’s wonder that God loved rebels through the crucified Christ.
Isaiah describes the Servant as rejected and bearing the sins of others. This gives biblical shape to the prayer’s confession that Jesus was despised, crucified, and carrying sin for his people.

sections.heading: Asking you to open my hard heart
sections.text: My heart can be cold and stubborn. Let your love soften what is hard in me and open what I keep locked shut. Father, I worship you for giving Jesus. Lord Jesus, I thank you for laying down your life for me. Holy Spirit, I thank you for making this good news real to me and not leaving it as words I could hear but never understand. Let Jesus see the fruit of his suffering in my life.
theological_themes: The human heart needs God’s gracious work to be softened and opened.
The Father gives the Son, the Son gives himself, and the Spirit reveals Christ to the believer.
Christ’s saving suffering bears fruit in those he redeems.

scripture_references.connection: God promises to replace a heart of stone with a living heart and to put his Spirit within his people. This directly supports the prayer’s plea for God to soften and open a resistant heart.

Paul teaches that the Spirit enables believers to understand what God has freely given them. This fits the prayer’s thanksgiving that the Spirit reveals the mystery of Christ rather than leaving the sinner blind to it.

The suffering Servant is promised that he will see the outcome of his suffering and be satisfied. The prayer echoes this by asking that Christ’s work would bear visible fruit in the life of the one praying.

sections.heading: Turning from false confidence to Christ alone
sections.text: Pull me away from every false thing I lean on, and bring me to rest in Christ alone. Do not let me treat his worth as something ordinary. Do not let me be unmoved by his blood. Make me want the cleansing only he can give, and make me honest about how deeply I need it.
theological_themes: Salvation rests in Christ alone, not in human merit or self-made security.
Christ’s blood cleanses the conscience and removes guilt.
True faith includes a serious desire to be cleansed, not merely excused.

scripture_references.connection: Paul rejects every ground of confidence apart from being found in Christ with the righteousness that comes through faith. This supports the prayer’s movement away from false trusts and toward Christ alone.

Hebrews presents Christ’s blood as able to purify the conscience for service to the living God. This grounds the prayer’s desire not to be indifferent to Christ’s blood but to seek real cleansing through him.

sections.heading: Giving myself wholly to my Redeemer
sections.text: Lord Jesus, my Master, Redeemer, and Savior, come and take full possession of me. You bought me; I belong to you. Hold me in your love and overcome my stubborn will. Take every part of me—my mind, my desires, my words, my hands, my plans—and make them holy and useful to you.
theological_themes: Believers belong to Christ because he purchased them by his death.
Christ’s loving lordship subdues the will without ceasing to be love.
Sanctification includes the whole person being set apart for God’s use.

scripture_references.connection: Paul tells believers that they are not their own because they were bought with a price, and therefore must glorify God with their bodies. This directly supports the prayer’s surrender of the whole self to Christ by right of purchase.
Paul urges believers, in view of God’s mercies, to present their bodies as a living sacrifice. This illuminates the prayer’s desire for every faculty and action to be consecrated to God.

sections.heading: Remembering how you have not failed me
sections.text: I am not ashamed of the hope I have placed in you. Trusting you has not left me disgraced. I brought you my countless sins, and you put them away. I trusted you when trouble surrounded me, and you brought me into a spacious place. I trusted you in distress, even when my faith was shaking, and you did not fail me.
theological_themes: Hope in God is not finally put to shame.
God forgives sins and removes guilt from his people.
God’s faithfulness holds the believer even when faith is weak and trembling.

scripture_references.connection: Paul connects justification, hope, suffering, endurance, and God’s love poured into believers’ hearts through the Spirit. This supports the prayer’s confidence that hope in God does not end in shame, even through distress.
Hezekiah speaks of God putting his sins behind his back after deliverance. This is an apt background for the prayer’s gratitude that God has dealt decisively with innumerable sins.
David remembers God drawing him out of overwhelming danger and bringing him into a broad place. This supports the prayer’s testimony that God delivered him when troubles closed in.

sections.heading: Adoring the God who chose, bought, and called me
sections.text: God of eternal mercy, God who chose me before I ever chose you, God who bought back what sin had ruined through the cross of Christ, God who called me with power I could not create in myself—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, I worship you. Glory, honor, majesty, power, and dominion belong to you forever. Amen.
theological_themes: Salvation begins in God’s electing grace, is accomplished through Christ’s cross, and is applied by God’s effective call.
The triune God receives worship for the whole work of redemption.
Christian assurance rests in God’s initiative and power, not in human self-rescue.

scripture_references.connection: This passage traces salvation from the Father’s choosing, through redemption in Christ’s blood, to the sealing work of the Holy Spirit. It strongly supports the prayer’s final Trinitarian praise for election, purchase, and calling.
Paul links God’s foreknowledge, predestination, calling, justification, and glorification as one saving work of God. This grounds the prayer’s adoration of God’s eternal choice and effectual call.
Jude ends with worship to the God who is able to keep his people and bring them safely into glory. This fits the prayer’s closing doxology of majesty, power, and dominion.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original explicitly includes doctrines often associated with Reformed theology, especially eternal election and effectual calling. These were preserved rather than softened, because they are central to the prayer’s closing praise.

The language of Christ’s ‘right by purchase’ assumes a redemption/ransom framework: believers belong to Christ because he bought them by his blood. This is biblical language but can sound possessive in modern ears, so it was rendered as loving lordship and belonging to Christ rather than bare ownership.

The phrase ‘let thy Son see in me the travail of his soul’ depends on Isaiah 53 and older language about Christ’s suffering. It was rendered as a request that Jesus would see the fruit of his suffering in the believer’s life.
significant_interpretive_choices: ‘Heaven’s darling’ was interpreted as referring to Jesus as the Father’s beloved Son, avoiding sentimental language while preserving the contrast between his divine belovedness and his humiliation for sinners.

‘In him thy grace has almost out-graced itself’ was not reproduced literally. It was rendered as God’s grace going beyond what the believer could imagine, preserving the sense of astonishment without implying that God exceeds himself in a strict theological sense.
‘My heart is locked’ was kept as a concrete image of inner resistance and closedness, rather than turned into a general request for emotional openness.
‘Wealthy place’ was interpreted through the biblical idea of being brought into a broad or spacious place after distress, rather than as material prosperity.
